status.label: Duplicate of the Grab and Move Win-modifier conflict
status.detail: The requested follow-up confirms the same Grab and Move/Win-key interaction already tracked by #47585.

next_action.label: Post a duplicate-triage note
next_action.reason: The author supplied the modifier and workaround details that the maintainer requested, so parallel fix work would duplicate #47585.

judgment.rationale: The author confirmed the exact distinguishing evidence requested by the maintainer: the problem remains reproducible with Grab and Move enabled using the Windows modifier, and disabling then re-enabling Grab and Move restores the shortcut. That matches the already-linked Grab and Move/Win-key conflict tracked in #47585, with #49127 also cross-referenced as the same family.
evidence: The original report maps Win+A to Win+N and describes the remap working only in Explorer/Desktop or not opening the Calendar pane.
The author later confirmed the issue is reproducible in PowerToys 0.100.2, Grab and Move is enabled with the Windows modifier, and disabling then re-enabling Grab and Move restores the shortcut.
A separate reporter confirmed in PowerToys 0.101.2373 that Win-based shortcuts fail while Grab and Move is enabled.
Maintainer guidance explicitly stated that this evidence would identify #47585, and #47585 now cross-references #47760.
Issue #47585 remains open and describes the same Win-modifier interaction affecting Keyboard Manager and other Win-key hotkeys; #49127 is also linked as the same conflict family.

No merged or open fix PR specifically covers the remapping defect. Open draft PR #49746 addresses Start opening after a Win-modified drag, which is related input handling but not a demonstrated fix for this report.
judgment.recommended_action: Post a specific duplicate-triage note linking #47760 to #47585, retain the reproduction details there, and do not start a competing design.

fix_assessment.rationale: This report is a confirmed duplicate of the open Grab and Move/Win-key tracking issue #47585. The related issue is the appropriate place for any code fix; no separate fix plan should be created here.

issue_context.summary: Keyboard Manager Win-key remaps intermittently fail when Grab and Move is configured to use the Windows key. The author confirmed the modifier and a toggle workaround, matching the existing Grab and Move conflict tracked in #47585.
known_information: The report is open and labeled Issue-Bug, Product-Keyboard Shortcut Manager, and Needs-Triage.
The original reproduction uses a Keyboard Manager Win+A to Win+N remap and reports partial or absent behavior outside Explorer/Desktop.
The author confirmed the problem in PowerToys 0.100.2 with Grab and Move enabled and its modifier set to Windows.
Disabling and re-enabling Grab and Move temporarily restores the shortcut.
Other commenters reproduced Win-based shortcut failures, including Win+O, while Grab and Move is enabled.
The maintainer asked for the modifier and whether disabling Grab and Move helps, then stated that a positive result identifies #47585.
Issue #47585 is open, explicitly covers Grab and Move with the Win key affecting other Win-key hotkeys, and cross-references #47760.
Current Grab and Move code in src/modules/GrabAndMove/GrabAndMove/main.cpp absorbs a Win keydown, tracks held non-modifier keys, and replays the modifier when no drag occurs.
The current source history includes open draft PR #49746 for a related Win-modified drag/Start-menu input issue, but it does not cover the Keyboard Manager remap behavior.
inferences: The temporary toggle recovery is consistent with Grab and Move hook state or input-order state being reset, but it does not prove which state transition is defective.

The shared failure across Keyboard Manager, Command Palette, and other Win-key hotkeys suggests the issue belongs to the common Grab and Move Win-key interception path rather than to one Keyboard Manager mapping.
The existence of related work does not establish that #47585 is fixed; it establishes that a duplicate report should not receive an independent implementation plan.
issue_context.analysis: The latest author response supplies the exact follow-up requested by the maintainer and makes the duplicate relationship actionable. The source path is technically consistent with the symptom: Grab and Move's KeyboardProc swallows and later replays Win input while maintaining per-hold state, so a shared input-hook defect can affect multiple consumers. Because #47585 is open and already tracks that behavior, the safe dashboard action is a duplicate-triage note rather than a competing fix design.
initial_investigation: Read the complete issue body and all eight public comments, including the maintainer request and the author's latest confirmation.
Checked the issue timeline: #47585 cross-references #47760, and #49127 cross-references #47585 as the same Grab and Move/Win-key conflict family.

Reviewed src/modules/GrabAndMove/GrabAndMove/main.cpp, especially KeyboardProc, the Win-key handling branch, g_heldNonAltKeyCount, g_winAbsorbed, g_pendingModifierReplayed, and ReplayAbsorbedModifier. The hook suppresses Win keydown in Win-modifier mode and replays it when no drag is completed.
Compared related reports #47585, #49127, and completed issue #47271. The reports share the same modifier-interception symptom; none supplies a separate fix for #47760.
Reviewed open draft PR #49746. Its stated scope is preventing Start activation after a Win-modified drag, not preserving Keyboard Manager Win-key remaps.

actions.label: Post duplicate-triage note linking #47585

comment.body: Thanks for confirming that this is still reproducible in PowerToys 0.100.2 with Grab and Move enabled and its modifier set to the Windows key, and that disabling then re-enabling Grab and Move restores the shortcut. Those details match the Win-key interception problem already tracked in #47585 (also related to #49127), including the effect on other Win-based hotkeys. Please consolidate any further reproduction details and fix discussion there so the same Grab and Move input-hook defect is not investigated twice.
